name: South Peak via Lookout

pitch_detail.notes: Long forest/subalpine trail; the modern approach adds a closed-road walk/bike before the historic trailhead.
Meadow and talus trail to the last camp before the glacier.
pitch_detail.pitch: Goat Flats to Tin Can Gap

pitch_detail.notes: Ice axe and crampons required; crevasse hazard.
pitch_detail.pitch: Tin Can Gap across the Queest-Alb Glacier edge

pitch_detail.notes: Three fixed ladders (rebar/timber anchored) gain the blasted summit block and L-4 lookout cabin at ~6,850 ft.

rappels: None typically — parties down-climb the ladders and glacier edge rather than rappel
descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no roped rappelling on the standard line. Downclimb the three fixed ladders in reverse (facing in, one at a time, mind the awkward 2nd-to-3rd ladder transition), then reverse the rock/snow scramble back down to and across the Queest-Alb Glacier, watching the moat and any open crevasses. Climb back up to Tin Can Gap and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. The main descent hazards are the exposed ladder pitch (a fall here would be very serious despite no technical rappelling), a soft or icy glacier moat later in the day, and lingering steep snow on the south ridge in early season — an ice axe is recommended into mid-summer. No rappel gear is needed for the standard route.
approach: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. From the Tupso Pass trailhead, follow Three Fingers Trail #641 through forest to Saddle Lake (~2.5 mi, last easy water — no fires or camping within 200 ft of the lake past this point), then continue up through meadows to Goat Flats (~4.5 mi total), a broad subalpine bench with the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail climbs roughly 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2-7 mi total, most of the day's 4,200 ft gain banked); this is where the maintained trail effectively ends and most casual hikers turn around. Beyond the gap, drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier — a short but real glacier crossing with a moat between ice and rock that widens through the season (crampons/axe strongly recommended, especially before August); a rope is worth carrying if crevasses are open. On the far side, scramble up rock and snow past the base of the summit block to the historic lookout's ladder system: three fixed wooden ladders bolted/pinned into the rock, stacked in sequence, gaining the final class-5-equivalent rock band to the lookout deck. The transition between the second and third ladder is the trickiest move and is awkward with a full pack; exposure is significant and a slip here would be serious, so this last pitch is why the route is rated a scramble rather than a hike despite no rope typically being used. Some parties fix or find a hand-line/rope on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier — treat it as unverified fixed gear.
overview: A long, storied outing to the historic fire lookout perched on the South Peak of Three Fingers, crossing the Queest-Alb Glacier. The L-4 gable lookout was built 1930-1932 by Darrington-area mountaineers Harold Engles and Frank Benesh (with Harry Bedal having assisted in the 1929 feasibility scout), staffed seasonally from 1933 through 1942, later rebuilt by volunteers, and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1987 — roughly the top 15 feet of the summit block was blasted flat to seat the cabin. It remains one of the most iconic hike-scrambles in the Cascade foothills, thanks largely to the three vertical ladders cabled to the final summit tower.
beta: This is the line Harry Bedal, Harold Engles, and Frank Benesh used to reach the South Peak summit to build the fire lookout in the early 1930s, and it remains the standard way up. From the trailhead the route follows trail to Saddle Lake, Goat Flats, and Tin Can Gap, then crosses the edge of the Queest-Alb Glacier before a rock scramble and a set of three fixed ladders (rebar and timber anchored into steep rock) gain the summit block and lookout. It is popular as a long day trip or, more commonly, an overnight from Goat Flats or Tin Can Gap given the approach length.
gear: Helmet for the glacier and scramble sections
Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass for trailhead parking
Headlamp — many parties start before dawn given the long day
fa: Harry Bedal, Harold Engles & Frank Benesh, c. 1929-1933 (route used to construct the fire lookout)
